title: Bonds- The Voldemort of Asset Allocation - Systematic Investor 320

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Bonds- The Voldemort of Asset Allocation - Systematic Investor 320.docx

speakers: Andrew Beer (co-founder, DBi, managed futures replication)
Alan Dunne (host, standing in for Niels Kaastrup-Larsen)
summary: Andrew Beer discusses trend-following performance in 2024, the structure and distribution of the CTA industry, managed futures ETFs and replication, and bonds as the diversifier that stopped working. Main conclusions: trend returns are noisy, replication and mutual funds track the industry closely, and 60/40 is shifting toward 50/30/20.

coverage.note: intro, disclaimers, guest small talk, US election opinion; no method content
October CTA performance, narrative shifts 2015-2022, medium to long-term trend as alpha
frustrating 18-24 months of oscillations, macro to performance link, Trump trade and head fakes
bond bettors underperformed cash; Hedge Nordic roundtable on industry structure
solutions business, allocators, no cannibalisation by replication
allocator decision criteria, no AUM growth
marketing vs real allocator behaviour, private equity marks, skill claims
manager narrative changes, ETF bucket constraints; setup of capital guarantee question
capital guaranteed products and regulatory reasons they faded
coupons vs duration, autocallables, return stacking, Millennium perception
liquid alts failure, survivorship, spaghetti cannon
complexity vs Sharpe, ETF vs mutual fund, Simplify ETF example
Man mutual fund vs ETF, statistical proof needs 10 years, 98% correlation mutual fund category
2022 return gap from fund constraints, replication accuracy logic
replication correlation and hit rate, competing replicators' enhancements; first-mover aside
replication as a tool, QIS and financial engineering
ETF flows, S&P opportunity cost, bonds as diversifier history
bond drawdown and vol repricing, 60/40 shift, models, stacking risks

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - core macro/bond and replication claims caught; misses were mostly secondary industry/structuring points (unbundled guarantees, front-running, ETF-vs-index numbers, allocator behaviour).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the sock chain CTA index was down 1.97%
claims.claim: October 2024 was a poor month for CTAs (SG CTA about -1.97%, SG Trend about -2.8% to 30 Oct), with month-end equity reversals making it worse and YTD trend turning negative despite the cash yield cushion.
claims.indicator: SG CTA Index, SG Trend Index

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: there were commoditized products coming into Trend and so people tended to to want to emphasize things that were non- Trend
claims.claim: Around 2015-16, as trend products became commoditized, managers pushed non-trend strategies; the narrative then flipped when trend did best in March 2020, 2021 and 2022, so narratives follow recent performance.
claims.testable: partly - narrative claim, performance by year is checkable

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the real source of alpha generation I and I believe this over time for reasons we can talk about is medium to long-term Trend
claims.claim: The speaker believes medium- to long-term trend is the real driver of returns in the managed futures space.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the oscillation are like are timed almost perfectly that by the time you start to love a trade
claims.claim: In the past 18-24 months, oscillations (BoJ, the Harris swap, Trump trade) reversed trades just as trend positions built up, making this one of the most frustrating years for medium- to long-term trend.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it just shows you how hard it is to translate a macro picture into um into performance
claims.claim: In late 2022 the CTA 5-year returns and macro backdrop (volatile inflation, rising rates) looked ideal, yet performance did not follow, so a macro narrative does not reliably predict strategy returns.
claims.testable: yes - macro regimes vs CTA returns

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: one of the great things about the space is they get out right they don't hold things with a white knuckle grip
claims.claim: Trend followers cut losing positions without attachment, which is a virtue but means they get hurt by head fakes when the market quickly reverses back.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's going to be good for equities it's going to be bad for bonds because you know because of uh tariffs
claims.claim: In July 2024 the Trump trade (long equities and dollar, short bonds because of tariffs and deficits) looked right, but the Biden-Harris swap and BoJ move reversed it.
claims.direction: Long equities, long dollar, short bonds

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: then SVP happens and rates are going down but for the wrong reasons because we think we're going to have a global banking crisis
claims.claim: Directional bond bets also suffered in 2023-24: the year of the bond turned into rates rising, then falling for banking-crisis reasons, then rising again, so bonds underperformed cash.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the big players in this space are in a very very privileged position in that they have great long-standing relationships with
claims.claim: From the Hedge Nordic roundtable: large CTAs hold a privileged position through long-standing relationships with sophisticated investors, which shapes how the industry gets assets.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you cannot believe how much of our business is Solutions based
claims.claim: A senior Man Group contact said much of their business is solutions-based, reflecting that allocators want a manager plus research support, not just a product.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's really impossible to make to to feel like you have an an edge in making that call
claims.claim: Nobody can call which strategies (alternative vs traditional, short vs long term) will work over the next three years, so the industry moved toward solutions and relationships.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: this loyal stable core of institutional allocators and you know in hedge fund World you'd say it's about 300 billion in assets
claims.claim: A loyal core of institutional allocators of roughly 300 billion in hedge fund assets has decade-long relationships, which is a stable but not growing asset base.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if the whole metric was is it better to own the S&P 500 versus a taking a shot at picking a long only active managers you would have picked the S&P 500 20 years ago
claims.claim: Investors keep paying active managers even though an index would have won, so replication will not cannibalise the industry: allocators want to talk to people picking strategies.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: not about incremental sharp ratio it's often not even really bad like there there's things that people throw out about it but it's it's do I make your life better right
claims.claim: Allocator decisions depend on whether a product fits their job and portfolio configuration, not on a 0.1-0.2 Sharpe difference.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the space hasn't grown on on the hedge fund side and the mutual fund side in a decade basically
claims.claim: Managed futures has not grown in a decade, creating zero-sum competition for a finite pool of assets.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: people walk in the room they say I want the best manager with the lowest fees the highest sharp ratio that does the best in a crisis
claims.claim: Stated allocator criteria (lowest fees, highest Sharpe, best in a crisis) describe a manager that does not exist and do not drive the real decision.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's the thing clients love most about it yes the volatil
claims.claim: In 2022 private equity funds did not mark down much because clients valued the smoothed marks, showing smoothing is valued when other portfolio parts are under stress (a dig at reported low volatility).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we've gone through six months of outperformance it wasn't luck
claims.claim: Fund marketing presents short outperformance as skill, which pulls in investors who are then disappointed, so the space does not grow.
claims.testable: partly - track record length vs noise

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if some if a manager uh makes a change to their system and then suddenly has better performance you know obviously it's probably more likely to be random
claims.claim: Better performance after a system change is more likely random, yet the change-and-it-works narrative resonates with investors.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the reason they would never invest in an ETF is because they're not going to have hedge fund
claims.claim: Consultants avoid hedge fund ETFs because their reporting buckets require a hedge fund category, a structural constraint on adoption, not performance.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: bought a zero coupon Bond and then the rest was uh spent on an option uh basically to track the performance
claims.claim: Capital-guaranteed CTA notes (zero-coupon bond plus option on a CTA program, as at Man AHL) only work when interest rates are high enough to leave money for the option, so they disappeared in the low-rate decade.
claims.indicator: zero-coupon bond plus option on CTA index
claims.testable: yes - price of the structure at given rates

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the self-regulatory organizations at some point decided that this wasn't really a bond this was a zeroc coupon Bond plus a hedge fund strategy
claims.claim: Principal-protected notes lost their main buyer, insurance companies, because regulators/accounting treated them as bond plus hedge fund, not as a bond.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: why would I do anything but buy short-term guilts and um you know I don't want duration risk
claims.claim: After years of low rates, wealth managers prefer short-dated gilts and coupons over duration or zero-coupon structures, so multi-strat UCITS have lost assets.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Auto cable so basically selling selling volatility and betting that you know certain ba certain stocks or baskets of stocks wouldn't trade below a certain level
claims.claim: Autocallable structured products, effectively selling volatility on equity baskets, stayed popular as rates rose because total return is higher.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they are all different representations of um combining different financial instruments
claims.claim: Return stacking and capital guarantee are both ways to combine instruments (bond plus option, or bond plus futures) to deliver exposure.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: those guys have done a sharp ratio of 2 plus for 30 years
claims.claim: A Millennium-type Sharpe of 2+ for 30 years feeds the perception that hedge funds are magical alpha machines, which shapes how liquid alternatives are judged.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you're talking like a 2% return over a decade right so maybe less than bonds over that period of time
claims.claim: Mutual fund and UCITS liquid alts returned about 2% a year over a decade after about 200 bp of fees, with high equity correlation (Wilshire data), a failed experiment.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you want to evaluate a space dig up all the dead bodies
claims.claim: To evaluate a space you must include closed funds, not just today's biggest five, to avoid survivorship bias.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you shoot enough spaghetti at the wall a couple pieces will stick
claims.claim: Firms launch about 12 products (the spaghetti cannon) so there is always a winner to push, and sales incentives (fees up to 170-200 bp) drive flows toward recent winners.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: there's not a lot of evidence that wildly more complexity meaningfully improves Sharps ratios in the space
claims.claim: Complexity does not meaningfully improve Sharpe in managed futures, so a simple ETF can work; the ETF wrapper does not hinder trend as it would an activist fund.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they seem to be killing it they're killing it this year like everyone goes down one day they seem to be going up
claims.claim: An idiosyncratic CTA ETF (Simplify) was doing well in 2024 even when peers fell, as evidence ETFs can do well.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they're going to dial up their risk controls a little bit more to be a little bit better at the inflection points
claims.claim: Man's mutual fund is designed as a diversified single line item with tighter risk controls to do better at inflection points, versus a wilder ETF.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: to actually prove that I think you need I don't know the exact number but I think it's 10 years of data or something like that
claims.claim: A Sharpe difference of 0.1-0.2 between a mutual fund and an ETF takes about 10 years to prove, so track records for new products are weak evidence and narratives matter.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you take the Morning Star us Trend systematic category you compared to the sogen CTA index and they have a 98% correlation to each other
claims.claim: Morningstar US systematic trend mutual funds correlate 98% with the SG CTA Index, so mutual funds deliver nearly identical performance.
claims.indicator: Morningstar US Systematic Trend category vs SG CTA Index

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the mutual funds after 20 170 basis points go up 14 so you lost something you lost 10 points because of your EV controls
claims.claim: In 2022 the SG CTA Index rose about 20-26% while mutual funds after 170 bp fees rose about 14%, ten points lost to controls; other periods nearly identical, about 200 bp a year over five years.
claims.indicator: SG CTA vs mutual fund returns 2022

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we are making one we bets that what we discern to be the broad Factor position in of the space on Monday afternoon will be sufficiently accurate
claims.claim: Replication bets that the factor positioning of the industry estimated on Monday is accurate enough for the following week, with a structural cost and fee advantage.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: using monthly dates about a 90% correlation
claims.claim: The replication tracks CTA performance with about 90% correlation on monthly returns.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you look at the weekly data we outperform somewhere between 53 and 54% of the time with a very very slightly positive skill
claims.claim: Weekly win rate vs the industry is 53-54%, which compounds to the 60s monthly, 70s quarterly and about 80% yearly, like a poker player's slight edge.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what most people are doing is looking at you know 150 days versus 20-day windows and I can add in more instruments
claims.claim: Competing replicators combine top-down replication with their own signals (150-day vs 20-day windows, more instruments) because backtests show better results, partly for commercial differentiation.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: replication will just be a tool in the same way that Q products are a tool
claims.claim: In five years replication will be a tool delivered through QIS swap products, ETFs and UCITS, showing financial engineering layered over the underlying strategy.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: one of the interesting things about an ETF that actually appeals to people it's easy to f a manager
claims.claim: ETFs make it easy to fire a manager because there is no relationship pressure, unlike hedge funds and mutual funds.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you just sell an alternative strategy today it's so hard to get anybody to care because the S&P is up 23%
claims.claim: With the S&P up 23%, investors will not give up beta for alternatives (opportunity cost), pushing AQR, Acadian and others toward 130/30 and return stacking.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it has a sharp ratio of 0.9 it's liquid has a negative correlation to equities
claims.claim: For 20 years the Bloomberg Aggregate bond index had Sharpe 0.9, negative equity correlation, 350 bp over cash and a max drawdown of 3.8% at 3-4% vol, which made bonds the superb diversifier.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the performance of bonds this decade have been um if this was an active manager been fired
claims.claim: Bonds are the Voldemort of asset allocation: a cornerstone of nearly every portfolio but with performance this decade that would get an active manager fired.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: every asset allocator is going to say what's what's my draw down potential in bonds and it's always going to be 16% not 4% or something
claims.claim: After large bond drawdowns allocators will assume a drawdown potential near 16%, not 4%, because financial history cannot be erased.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the V of of like corporate Bonds in the US may be higher than the sgct right now like it's it's up into the it's gone from 4 to 8 or 9 or 10 or something
claims.claim: US corporate bond volatility may have risen from about 4 to 8-10, possibly above the SG CTA Index, so models for the next 10 years cannot assume 4% bond vol.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: bonds are under performing cash again the third year in a row not the second year in a row
claims.claim: Bonds underperformed cash for a third year in a row in 2024.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: this shift from the ease of 6040 where everything was working for you all the time to something looks like 5030 20 is is is happening
claims.claim: Allocators are shifting from 60/40 to roughly 50/30/20 with the 20% in assets uncorrelated to stocks and bonds (infrastructure, private credit, private equity, managed futures).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the model is never going to give you an answer that you want so you're like okay let's not do that
claims.claim: Asset allocation models need judgment, haircuts and parameter constraints, so they contain much narrative and art as well as science.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the risk is that when you package it together your skis are pointing the same direction you go through unexpectedly large draw downs
claims.claim: Stacking capital-efficient overlays on top of other assets risks unexpectedly large drawdowns when the legs fall together, and investors' drawdown tolerance is less than they say.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you invested a manager you had a bad experience with it 3 years ago and and the decision was to get out of the space entirely your view is going to be completely different
claims.claim: Allocators' views of managed futures depend heavily on their own past experience: one bad manager experience often leads to exiting the whole space, while others internalise the strategy or move to QIS.
claims.testable: no - allocator decision history is not observable

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: people think we are very strange for being proud of not changing what we do in eight plus years
claims.claim: In contrast to managers who sell a 'we changed the system and it works' story, Beer keeps his replication process unchanged for eight-plus years and treats that stability as a virtue.
claims.testable: partly - live record since an unchanged-process date can be evaluated out of sample

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you want to sell that to retail I'm not sure it's still regarded as it's still regarded as complex because the underlying investment is is seen as complex
claims.claim: Capital-guaranteed CTA notes may also have faded because retail regulation still classes them as complex products, since the underlying strategy is seen as complex despite the guarantee.
claims.testable: no - regulatory classification, not a market series

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: nobody's spending a lot of time analyzing the all-in cost of these things they can charge huge commissions on it
claims.claim: Principal-protected products sold to wealthy clients (e.g. in Latin America) are loaded with fees and commissions whose all-in cost buyers rarely analyse, which gives them a poor reputation.
claims.testable: partly - all-in cost of structured notes can be computed from term sheets

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we want to do 300 million but we want to put up 100 million of you know we want to manage the bond portfolio
claims.claim: Large institutions now unbundle guaranteed structures: they take a managed futures program at e.g. 300 million notional on 100 million of margin and manage the bond/collateral portfolio themselves, getting the same result without a stapled bond.
claims.conditions: institutions able to run their own collateral

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they'll pick one of the five probably not the best because he might be a little bit too crazy probably not the worst
claims.claim: For ease, social validation and career risk, allocators choose among the five largest managers in a space and typically pick a middle one (not the best, not the worst) rather than evaluating the full universe.
claims.testable: partly - flows by manager size and performance rank

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it kind of fed into this narrative of ah the reason was because they're mutual funds it was a mistake to go look for liquidity
claims.claim: The poor liquid-alts record was wrongly blamed on the liquid (mutual fund) wrapper, when the real cause was traditional managers pushing high-fee products they did not know how to run.
claims.testable: partly - compare liquid-alt returns by sponsor type and fee level

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: somebody can calculate exactly how much of the heating oil Market you represent or something okay that gets a little bit scary from a front running perspective
claims.claim: Daily position transparency in an ETF is a real front-running risk only for very large managers whose share of a market can be calculated; for most CTAs the ETF wrapper is not a handicap.
claims.conditions: large manager with sizeable share of a futures market
claims.testable: partly - trading costs around ETF rebalance dates

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the the CTA s CTA trending it's down 11 they're down four right
claims.claim: Since AlphaSimplex launched its managed futures ETF, the SG CTA trend index fell about 11% while the ETF fell about 4%, evidence that an ETF need not lack risk controls.
claims.indicator: SG CTA Trend index vs AlphaSimplex managed futures ETF
claims.testable: yes - compare returns since ETF launch

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they expect a higher sharp because you've got Trend and other strategies and trading more Market market
claims.claim: The usual argument (put by the host) is that a fund combining trend with other strategies and more markets should, all else equal, have a higher Sharpe than a pure-trend ETF; Beer disputes that complexity adds much Sharpe.
claims.testable: yes - compare Sharpe of diversified vs pure-trend CTA products

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I think investors can stomach more volatility to a certain point
claims.claim: Replicating pre-incentive-fee returns makes the product more volatile than net-of-fee CTA indices, which Beer argues investors can accept up to a point in exchange for the higher return.
claims.testable: partly - compare volatility of replicators vs CTA indices
